terminal.description: A shell in your workspace. Build the repair bill here, run it, and read what it prints.

tasks.title: Price the labour
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 1` in `src/prices.cpp`, make a `double` called `labour`: the hourly rate times the hours worked. Print it:

```
Labour: 115.5
```

Check runs your program with other rates and hours, reads `labour` and its type, and looks for the line.
nextSteps: Find `hourlyRate` and `hoursWorked` at the top of `main`, and note their types.
Make `labour` as a `double`, worked out from those two names.
Print `Labour: ` and then `labour`.
Build, run, and check the number against the slip: 38.5 for each of 3 hours.
hints: The labour is one number times another. Which operator multiplies in C++?
When a `double` and an `int` meet in a sum, the `int` is turned into a `double` first, so the result keeps its decimals.
The line has the shape `double labour = hourlyRate * ...;`.

tasks.title: Bag the screws
tasks.description:
Kasimir puts `screwsPerBag` screws in each bag. Under `// Task 2`, make an `int` called `fullBags`, the number of full bags the box of `screwsInBox` screws makes, and an `int` called `leftOver`, the screws left over. Print them:

```
Full bags: 3, left over: 2
```

Check runs your program with other boxes and bags, a box that comes out even and a box too small for one bag among them, and reads both variables and the line.
nextSteps: Work out today's numbers by hand: 14 screws, 4 to a bag.
Make `fullBags` by dividing the screws by the screws per bag.
Make `leftOver` with the operator that gives what is left after a division.
Print both on one line, build and run.
hints: Dividing one `int` by another gives an `int`: the whole part, with nothing after the point. That is exactly a count of full bags.
The `%` operator gives the remainder of a whole-number division: what is left once the full bags are packed.
The two lines have the shapes `int fullBags = screwsInBox / ...;` and `int leftOver = screwsInBox % ...;`.

tasks.title: Find the average job
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 3`, make a `double` called `averageMinutes`: `minutesTotal` divided by `jobsDone`, decimals included. Print it:

```
Average: 62.5 minutes
```

Check runs your program with other minutes and jobs, some that divide evenly and some that do not, and reads `averageMinutes` and the line.
nextSteps: Make `averageMinutes` the obvious way, build, run, and compare with 62.5.
Notice which types `minutesTotal` and `jobsDone` have.
Turn one of them into a `double` before the division happens.
Build and run: the half minute should be back.
hints: Putting the result into a `double` does not help if the division was already done in whole numbers.
The type of a division is decided by the numbers being divided. One `double` among them is enough to keep the decimals.
`static_cast<double>(minutesTotal)` is `minutesTotal` as a `double`. Divide that by `jobsDone`.

tasks.title: Count the beats of the guarantee
tasks.description:
A watch beats `beatsPerSecond` times a second, and the workshop's guarantee lasts `guaranteeYears` years of 365 days. Under `// Task 4`, make a `long long` called `guaranteeBeats`: how many times the watch beats in that time. Print it:

```
Beats: 2522880000
```

Check runs your program with other watches and guarantees, short ones and long ones, and reads `guaranteeBeats` and the line.
nextSteps: Work out the seconds in a day, then in a year of 365 days.
Make `guaranteeBeats` as a `long long`: beats a second, times seconds a year, times years.
Build and run with today's slip and compare with the task's number.
If it comes out wrong or below zero, read the part of the lesson on how big an `int` can get.
hints: A minute has 60 seconds, an hour 60 minutes, a day 24 hours, a year 365 days.
An `int` holds numbers up to a little over two billion. A multiplication of `int`s is worked out in `int`, even when the result goes into a `long long`, so it can run past the top first.
Make the first number of the multiplication a `long long`: `static_cast<long long>(beatsPerSecond) * 60 * ...`.

tasks.title: Print the parts price
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 5`, print `partsCost` with exactly two digits after the point:

```
Parts: 12.40
```

The tools for it are in a header this file does not include yet. Check runs your program with other prices, a whole number among them, and looks for the line.
nextSteps: Print `Parts: ` and `partsCost` plainly, build, run, and see what is wrong with it.
Read the part of the lesson on printing prices.
Add the `#include` line it needs at the top of the file.
Send `std::fixed` and `std::setprecision(2)` before the price, build and run.
hints: `std::cout` prints a `double` with as few digits as it can, so 12.40 comes out as 12.4.
`std::setprecision` lives in the header `<iomanip>`. On its own it counts every digit of the number; after `std::fixed`, it counts the digits after the point.
Add `#include <iomanip>` at the top, then send `std::fixed << std::setprecision(2)` to `std::cout` before `partsCost`.
